# ADHD-Friendly Responses

Shape responses so the reader can act without retaining context.

## Response contract

1. For a task, make the first sentence an imperative, sub-two-minute action; put no reassurance or context before it. For a question, give the direct answer. Never announce this skill.
2. Number multi-step work: one action per step, five items per visible list. Shape plans as `Now` (up to five actions plus a done condition), `Later` (one line of phase names), `State`, and `Next`. Expand nothing else.
3. Restate the current step and progress. Surface wins, defer tangents, and use concrete time estimates.
4. For errors, state failure, evidence or cause, and fix. After three failed attempts, name the suspect assumption and ask one diagnostic question.
5. End unfinished work with one imperative, sub-two-minute action and nothing after it. If complete, end with the verified outcome.

## Exceptions

- Explain fully when asked, using skimmable headings.
- Confirm destructive or irreversible actions.
- Ask one question for material ambiguity.
- Let safety, accuracy, and explicit instructions override brevity.

## Pre-send check

Remove announcements, closing pleasantries, tangents, empty hedging, and buried wins. Ensure the first and last lines carry the action or outcome.

# yyot v1 scope and build approach ## State **yyot v1 is a hosted Hermes-based Slack assistant for general browser tasks and access management. Reuse Hermes first; focus yyot-specific work on routing and authorization, and add code only for demonstrated gaps.** The repository currently contains Git/Entire scaffolding and this scope. No configured yyot runtime, deployed reviewer experience, or acceptance evidence exists yet. Upstream documentation establishes available capabilities, not that our chosen deployment has passed its requirements. The assignment permits third-party components and prioritizes a smooth working experience over code volume. A successful v1 may consist mostly of configuration, deployment, integration fixes, and verification. There is no requirement to build a new agent harness, Slack connector, browser engine, vault, or TOTP algorithm. Slack is the v1 interface. The user reported that Sahan approved Slack identity replacing the assignment's Google-only chatbot sign-in requirement. Sahan and Nishank enter through the demo workspace invitation/entry link and use yyot without local setup or their own model-provider accounts. Inference is owner-funded. The assignment's core is browser tasks and secure access management. Private DMs, shared channel context, and protection between reviewers are additional v1 behavior requested by the user. A general self-service SaaS platform is not a prerequisite. ## Reuse from Hermes Pin the Hermes version and required integrations, configure them, and verify their behavior in the deployed Slack experience. | Capability | Starting point | What yyot must establish | | --- | --- | --- | | Agent harness | Hermes's agent loop, tools, skills, and session machinery | General tasks work with the selected model and enabled tools. | | Slack interface | Hermes's existing Slack adapter and gateway | App configuration, authenticated admission, correct conversation routing, and replies. | | Browser automation | Existing Browser Use integration and supported browser backends | Background browser work, file workflows, independent sessions, and saved-access reuse. | | Credentials and 2FA | Hermes's credential vault, protected browser filling, TOTP support, and access-management controls | Reviewers can securely provide, reuse, and remove access through the hosted experience. Resolve the TOTP choice below. | | Profiles and conversations | Existing profile routing, DM/channel/thread sessions, memory, and persistence | The selected configuration enforces the intended tenant, owner, and audience boundaries across turns and restarts. | Start from the documented [browser integration](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/), [credential vault](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/credential-vault/), [profile routing](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/multi-profile-gateways/#routing-shared-bot-chats-to-profiles-profile_routes), and [session behavior](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions). Native vault documentation shows interactive CLI/Desktop flows; a complete secure Slack collection and revocation flow still needs validation. Treat that as a check, not proof that a new credential service is required. ## Architecture and routing contract **Start by evaluating one shared Hermes deployment serving separate conversations and profiles.** Neither a permanent instance per user nor an instance per tenant is required by this scope. Profiles and sessions organize state; the deployment and tool configuration must enforce the required access boundaries. Introduce additional processes or sandboxes where the chosen tools require them, based on evidence. ```mermaid flowchart TD Slack["Slack workspaces
Private DMs and shared channels/threads"] <--> Gateway["Hermes Slack gateway"] Gateway <--> Routing["Tenant, sender, context, and access routing
Use existing configuration first"] Routing <--> Private["Private conversations
Owner-scoped history and resources"] Routing <--> Shared["Shared conversations
Context scoped to channel audience"] Private <--> Tools["Existing Hermes tools
Authorized browser, vault, and file access"] Shared <-->|Only resources authorized for this shared turn| Tools ``` These boxes describe responsibilities, not mandatory new services. The routing checks may be Hermes configuration, supported extension points, or a small yyot integration. A separate custom gateway, authorization service, provisioner, or broker must earn its place by fixing a demonstrated gap. Run Hermes in its upstream runtime; TypeScript remains the preference for yyot-owned integration code where appropriate. | Routing decision | Required behavior | | --- | --- | | Tenant | Derive workspace/installation identity from authenticated Slack events. Include it in user, conversation, and resource routing. Reject unknown or unauthorized requesters instead of falling into a privileged default. | | Conversation and audience | A 1:1 DM loads that user's private context. A channel/thread loads context authorized for that channel's audience. Workspace membership alone does not reveal private-channel history. | | Requester and resource owner | Keep the sender, account/resource owner, and conversation audience distinct. Validate ownership before using credentials, browsers, files, history, or controls. Another participant's follow-up conveys no authority over someone else's private work. | | Context and tools | Scope memory, session recall, learned skills, files, artifacts, browser state, and credentials to the current authorized context. Prompt instructions and model-supplied owner IDs cannot grant access. | | Result destination | Return private account results privately. Sharing requires the owner's approval of the specific content and audience. Shared output grants no access to its source account or private files. | Session separation and profile routing are useful controls, but must be tested together with tools and persistence. Shared-profile memory or session recall must not expose DM content in a channel. Model-generated code must not have unrestricted access to other owners' files, the shared history store, or platform administrator credentials. Use supported scoped tools and isolated execution where needed; disable or adapt a tool whose access cannot be constrained. Keep retained history, recovery state, browser access, and artifacts durable across restarts, with their owner/audience associations intact. Use existing persistence when it meets these needs. Hosting, storage, and the exact profile/session mapping remain implementation choices; no particular cloud vendor, database, or object store is mandated. For v1 delivery, the reviewers use one demo workspace. Routing must still carry tenant identity and be checked against another tenant identity without requiring a public onboarding or provisioning product. ### Example: collaboration involving a private account Sahan and Nishank discuss a report in a shared thread. Both contributions belong to that thread's context. If the work needs Sahan's private account, route that part into an owner-authorized private conversation/run, using existing capabilities where possible. Obtain missing authorization through his DM or secure handoff. Private observations never enter the shared conversation automatically. Sahan receives the result privately and may approve selected content for publication back into the thread. Nishank can continue the shared discussion without gaining authority over Sahan's account. ## Required behavior 1. **Perform general browser and file tasks.** Accept natural-language goals across different, unfamiliar websites. Discover and upload an intended existing file; support download, inspection/transformation, and upload when requested. Site-specific scripts are not evidence of general capability. 2. **Collect, reuse, and revoke access.** Support secure input or login handoff for passwords, API keys, OAuth/browser access, and card details when needed. In the interactive CLI, dangerous commands show an inline approval prompt:

  2. DM pairing approved list (users approved via pairing codes)
  3. Platform-specific allowlists (e.g., `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS=12345,67890`)
  4. Global allowlist (`GATEWAY_ALLOWED_USERS=12345,67890`)

When the agent needs to ask you a multiple-choice question (the `clarify` tool), Slack renders it as Block Kit buttons — one tap per option, plus an "✏️ Other…" button that switches to free-text mode (your next typed message becomes the answer). After a tap, the message updates in place to show who answered and what was chosen; further clicks on the same prompt are ignored. Button clicks honor the same user authorization as messages, and expired prompts (gateway restart, timeout) tell you to re-ask instead of silently eating the click. Open-ended clarify questions render as a plain question and accept your next typed reply. No configuration needed — this works regardless of the `rich_blocks` setting.

Set `SLACK_HOME_CHANNEL` to a channel ID where Hermes will deliver scheduled messages, cron job results, and other proactive notifications. To find a channel ID:

### Cron delivery targeting​

Cron jobs (see the cron guide) can target Slack three ways:

`deliver:` value  | Where it lands
--- | ---
`slack`  | The home channel (`SLACK_HOME_CHANNEL`)
`slack:C0123456789`  | A specific channel by ID
`slack:U0123456789`  | That user's DM — the bare user ID is resolved to a DM conversation automatically (requires the `im:write` scope)

Delivery works even when the cron process isn't co-located with the gateway — Hermes falls back to a standalone Web API sender using `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`. `MEDIA:` attachments in the cron output are uploaded as native Slack file shares to the same target.

The agent's `send_message` tool accepts the same target shapes: a channel ID (`C…`/`G…`), a DM conversation (`D…`), or a bare user ID (`U…`/`W…`), which is resolved to the user's DM on every send path — text, media, and interactive prompts alike. `MEDIA:<path>` attachments (images, PDFs, documents) upload as native file shares; when a short message accompanies a single attachment it rides as the file's caption instead of a separate message. ## Multi-Workspace Support​

Hermes can connect to multiple Slack workspaces simultaneously using a single gateway instance. Each workspace is authenticated independently with its own bot user ID.

### Configuration​

Provide multiple bot tokens as a comma-separated list in `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`:
    
    `
    
    # Multiple bot tokens — one per workspace
    
    REDACTED,xoxb-workspace2-token,xoxb-workspace3-token
    
    # A single app-level token is still used for Socket Mode
    
    SLACK_APP_TOKEN=xapp-your-app-token
    
    `

Or in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
    
    `
    
    platforms:
    
      slack:
    
        token: "xoxb-workspace1-token,xoxb-workspace2-token"
    
    `

### OAuth Token File​

In addition to tokens in the environment or config, Hermes also loads tokens from an OAuth token file at:
    
    `
    
    ~/.hermes/slack_tokens.json
    
    `

This file is a JSON object mapping team IDs to token entries:
    
    `
    
    {
    
      "T01ABC2DEF3": {
    
        "token": "xoxb-workspace-token-here",
    
        "team_name": "My Workspace"
    
      }
    
    }
    
    `

Tokens from this file are merged with any tokens specified via `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`. Duplicate tokens are automatically deduplicated.

### How it works​

  * The first token in the list is the primary token, used for the Socket Mode connection (AsyncApp).
  * Each token is authenticated via `auth.test` on startup. The gateway maps each `team_id` to its own `WebClient` and `bot_user_id`.
  * When a message arrives, Hermes uses the correct workspace-specific client to respond.
  * The primary `bot_user_id` (from the first token) is used for backward compatibility with features that expect a single bot identity.

## Redirecting the Agent Mid-Turn​

While the agent is working, you can send a correction without starting a new turn:

  * Type a new message + Enter — redirects the active turn using your correction
  * `Ctrl+C` — interrupt the current operation (press twice within 2s to force exit)
  * Completed tool work and reasoning already shown stay in context
  * A running tool reaches its safe boundary before the correction is applied

### Busy Input Mode​

The `display.busy_input_mode` config key controls what happens when you press Enter while the agent is working:

Mode  | Behavior
--- | ---
`"interrupt"` (default)  | Your message redirects the active turn. Model generation restarts with displayed reasoning and completed work preserved. A running foreground terminal command is moved to the background (not killed — you get a completion notification) so your message is read immediately; other running tools finish first
`"queue"`  | Your message is silently queued and sent as the next turn after the agent finishes
`"steer"`  | Your message is injected into the current run via `/steer`, arriving at the agent after the next tool call — no interrupt, no new turn
    
    `
    
    # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
    
    display:
    
      busy_input_mode: "steer"   # or "queue" or "interrupt" (default)
    
    `

`"queue"` mode prepares a separate follow-up turn. `"steer"` always waits for the next tool-result boundary. The default `"interrupt"` mode responds sooner during model generation while avoiding cancellation of a running tool; a long foreground `terminal` command (a build, a poller) is handed to the background so the agent sees your message right away instead of after the command exits. Use `/stop` when you want to cancel the turn and its foreground work. Unknown values fall back to `"interrupt"`.

`"steer"` has two automatic fallbacks: if the agent hasn't started yet, or if images are attached, the message falls back to `"queue"` behavior so nothing is lost.

Whatever the mode, `/queue <prompt>` queues a follow-up turn explicitly, and `/queue list`, `/queue rm N`, `/queue edit N …` and `/queue move A B` act on the pending queue immediately, even mid-run. The live work dock lists what is waiting.

You can also change it inside the CLI:
    
    `
    
    /busy queue
    
    /busy steer
    
    /busy interrupt
    
    /busy status
    
    `

First-touch hint

The first time you press Enter while Hermes is working, Hermes prints a one-line reminder explaining the `/busy` knob. It only fires once per install; `onboarding.seen.busy_input_prompt` in `config.yaml` records that it was shown. Delete that key to see the tip again.

### Suspending to Background​

On Unix systems, press `Ctrl+Z` to suspend Hermes to the background — just like any terminal process. The shell prints a confirmation:
    
    `
    
    Hermes Agent has been suspended. Run `fg` to bring Hermes Agent back.
    
    `

Type `fg` in your shell to resume the session exactly where you left off. This is not supported on Windows.

## Background Sessions​

Run a prompt in a separate background session while continuing to use the CLI for other work:
    
    `
    
    /bg Analyze the logs in /var/log and summarize any errors from today
    
    `

Hermes immediately confirms the task and gives you back the prompt:
    
    `
    
    🔄 Background task #1 started: "Analyze the logs in /var/log and summarize..."
    
       Task ID: bg_143022_a1b2c3
    
    `

### How It Works​

Each `/bg` prompt spawns a completely separate agent session in a daemon thread:

  * Isolated conversation — the background agent has no knowledge of your current session's history. It receives only the prompt you provide.
  * Same configuration — the background agent inherits your model, provider, toolsets, reasoning settings, and fallback model from the current session.

Run a prompt in a separate background session so the agent works on it independently while your main chat stays responsive:
    
    `

### How It Works​

Each `/bg` prompt spawns a separate agent instance that runs asynchronously:

  * Isolated session — the background agent has its own session with its own conversation history. It has no knowledge of your current chat context and receives only the prompt you provide.
  * Same configuration — inherits your model, provider, toolsets, reasoning settings, and provider routing from the current gateway setup.
  * Non-blocking — your main chat stays fully interactive. Send messages, run other commands, or start more background tasks while it works.

L889: ## TLS certificate trustcite89†​ L890: 
L891: Hermes initializes the platform verifier through `truststore`. Windows uses its certificate store, macOS uses its system trust services, and Linux uses the OpenSSL system trust paths. If initialization fails, Hermes logs the failure and falls back to OpenSSL defaults.
L892: For a corporate TLS proxy, install its root through your organization's operating-system trust procedure. Hermes' provider resolver no longer selects trust through `HERMES_CA_BUNDLE` or the old CA-environment-variable ladder. Sandboxed subprocesses can have their own separate CA configuration.
L893: The former startup certificate guard is gone with it: Hermes no longer validates `HERMES_CA_BUNDLE` / `SSL_CERT_FILE` / `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` / `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` at launch, so there is no `SSLConfigurationError` and the `HERMES_SKIP_SSL_GUARD` escape hatch has no effect.
L894: `HERMES_CA_BUNDLE` is still honoured by the Nous Portal login flow only (`hermes login`, or its `--ca-bundle` flag); the standard `SSL_CERT_FILE` / `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE` / `CURL_CA_BUNDLE` variables are still read by the plain `requests`/`urllib` calls some tools make (and by `pip`, `uv`, `curl`, Node), so a stale path in one of them now fails at the call that uses it rather than at startup. Fix or unset the variable there.
L895: A custom provider can declare `ssl_ca_cert` for its endpoint. That bundle replaces platform trust for chat, model metadata, and model catalog probes. A missing file produces a warning and falls back to platform trust. `ssl_verify: false` disables certificate verification and is unsafe for untrusted networks. Do not use it as a permanent fix for a missing corporate root.

L674: ### Repair Stranded Gateway Sessionscite69†​ L675: 
L676: If a gateway conversation ever "jumps back in time" after a restart — resuming a days-old topic as though recent messages never happened — the live conversation may be stranded in a session row that lost its routing identity (the damage class fixed in the v0.21 session-continuity work; current versions prevent it by construction and self-heal at runtime).
L699: Anything ambiguous (two candidate predecessors, two orphans claiming the same predecessor) is reported with a reason and left untouched — a wrong adoption would splice one conversation into another chat. The superseded row is retired under `superseded_by_repair`, so restart recovery can never resurrect it.
L700: Repair is deliberately not automatic: if the chat has since built up a second history, choosing which thread it continues is your call. The stranded conversation stays readable via `/resume` and session search either way — routing is the only thing the repair changes. Back up first (`cp ~/.hermes/state.db ~/.hermes/state.db.bak`).
L701: ### Repair Degraded Stored Promptscite70†​ L702: 
L703: Older builds affected by #122822 could let gateway hygiene or gateway `/compress` persist a detached maintenance agent's reduced-toolset system prompt over the live session. After the root fix in PR #122825 is installed, use `hermes sessions repair-prompts` to find rows that were already degraded.
L704: The scan is conservative: it only proposes a repair when the stored prompt is missing the `## Skill Safety` guidance and the persisted `tools[]` pin contains `skill_manage` (which always emits that guidance). Rows with no readable pin, or with a `memory`-only pin (which is also a legitimate `toolsets: [memory]` setup), are reported as unverifiable and are not changed by this scan; clear them explicitly by `SESSION_ID` if needed.
L705: A memory-only row also becomes repairable on its own: once the session is resumed, its `tools[]` pin re-pins the full tool surface, after which a scan sees `skill_manage` without the Skill Safety guidance and clears it.

L44: # Security
L45: 
L46: Hermes Agent is designed with a defense-in-depth security model. This page covers every security boundary — from command approval to container isolation to user authorization on messaging platforms.
L47: ## Overviewcite33†​ L48: 
L49: The security model has eight layers:
L50:   1. User authorization — who can talk to the agent (allowlists, DM pairing)
L51:   2. Dangerous command approval — human-in-the-loop for destructive operations
L52:   3. File write safety — denylist and optional write sandbox for `write_file`/`patch`
L53:   4. Container isolation — Docker/Singularity/Modal sandboxing with hardened settings
L54:   5. MCP credential filtering — environment variable isolation for MCP subprocesses
L55:   6. Context file scanning — prompt injection detection in project files
L56:   7. Cross-session isolation — sessions cannot access each other's data or state; cron job storage paths are hardened against path traversal attacks
L57:   8. Input sanitization — working directory parameters in terminal tool backends are validated against an allowlist to prevent shell injection
L58: ## Dangerous Command Approvalcite34†​ L59: 
L60: Before executing any command, Hermes checks it against a curated list of dangerous patterns. If a match is found, the user must explicitly approve it.
L61: ### Approval Modescite35†​ L62: The approval system supports three modes, configured via `approvals.mode` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
L63: 
L64:     `
L65: 
L66:     approvals:
L67: 
L68:       mode: smart                     # smart | manual | off
L69: 
L70:       timeout: 300                    # seconds to wait for user response (default: 300)
L71: 
L72:       cron_mode: deny                 # deny | approve — what cron jobs do when they hit a dangerous command
L73:       single_query_mode: deny         # deny | approve — what single-query (-q) sessions do on a dangerous command
L74: 
L75:       unattended_mode: deny           # deny | approve — what webhook/API sessions do on a dangerous command
L76: 
L77:       mcp_reload_confirm: true        # /reload-mcp asks before invalidating the MCP tool cache
L78: 
L79:       destructive_slash_confirm: true # /clear, /new, /reset, /undo prompt before discarding state
L80: 
L81:     `
L82: The full set of keys:
L83: Key  | Default  | What it controls
L84: --- | --- | ---
L85: `mode`  | `smart`  | Approval policy for dangerous shell commands — see the table below.
L86: `timeout`  | `300`  | Seconds Hermes waits for an approval reply before timing out.
L87: `cron_mode`  | `deny`  | How cite36†cron jobs behave headlessly when they trigger a dangerous-command prompt. `deny` blocks the command (the agent must find another path); `approve` auto-approves everything in cron context.
L88: `single_query_mode`  | `deny`  | How one-shot cite5†`hermes chat -q` sessions behave when they trigger a dangerous-command prompt. A `-q` session runs a single turn and exits with no user waiting to answer prompts; `deny` blocks the command (the agent must find another path), `approve` auto-approves everything in single-query context. Mirrors `cron_mode`.
L89: `unattended_mode`  | `deny`  | How sessions on unattended programmatic platforms (webhook, msgraph_webhook, api_server) behave when they trigger a dangerous-command prompt. These surfaces have no human who can answer `/approve`, so instead of blocking for the full approval timeout, `deny` blocks the command instantly (the agent must find another path) and `approve` auto-approves everything in unattended context. Mirrors `cron_mode`.
L90: `mcp_reload_confirm`  | `true`  | When true, `/reload-mcp` asks before rebuilding the MCP tool set. Rebuilding invalidates the provider prompt cache (tool schemas live in the system prompt), so the next message re-sends full input tokens. Users who click Always Approve flip this key to `false`.
L91: `destructive_slash_confirm`  | `true`  | When true, destructive session slash commands (`/clear`, `/new`, `/reset`, `/undo`) prompt before discarding conversation state. Three-option dialog (Approve Once / Always Approve / Cancel) routed through native yes/no buttons on Telegram, Discord, and Slack; text fallback elsewhere. Users who click Always Approve flip this key to `false`.
L92: The TUI also honors this setting for its `/clear`, `/new`, and `/reset` modal; `HERMES_TUI_NO_CONFIRM=1` force-skips that modal regardless of the configured value.
L93: Mode  | Behavior
L94: --- | ---
L95: smart (default)  | Use an auxiliary LLM to assess risk. Low-risk commands (e.g., `python -c "print('hello')"`) are auto-approved for that command only. Genuinely dangerous commands are auto-denied. Uncertain cases escalate to a manual prompt.
L96: manual  | Always prompt the user for approval on dangerous commands.
L97: off  | Disable all approval checks — equivalent to running with `--yolo`. All commands execute without prompts.
L98: warning

L100: Setting `approvals.mode: off` disables all safety prompts. Use only in trusted environments (CI/CD, containers, etc.).
L101: ### YOLO Modecite37†​ L102: 
L103: YOLO mode bypasses all dangerous command approval prompts for the current session. It can be activated three ways:
L104: 
L105:   1. CLI flag: Start a session with `hermes --yolo` or `hermes chat --yolo`
L106:   2. Slash command: Type `/yolo` during a session to toggle it on/off
L107:   3. Environment variable: Set `HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1`
L108: The `/yolo` command is a toggle — each use flips the mode on or off:
L109: 
L110:     `
L111: 
L112:     > /yolo
L113: 
L114:       ⚡ YOLO mode ON — all commands auto-approved. Use with caution.
L115: 
L116:     > /yolo
L117: 
L118:       ⚠ YOLO mode OFF — dangerous commands will require approval.
L119: 
L120:     `

L122: YOLO mode is available in both CLI and gateway sessions. Internally, it sets the `HERMES_YOLO_MODE` environment variable which is checked before every command execution.
L123: When YOLO is active, Hermes shows two persistent visual reminders so it's hard to forget that approval prompts are bypassed:
L124: 
L125:   * A red banner line at session start when YOLO is already active: `⚠ YOLO mode — all approval prompts bypassed`. Hidden when YOLO is off so the default banner stays uncluttered.
L126:   * A `⚠ YOLO` fragment in the status bar across all width tiers, updated live as you toggle YOLO on or off (rich-text renderer and plain-text fallback).
L127: 
L128: danger
L129: YOLO mode disables all dangerous command safety checks for the session — except the hardline blocklist (see below). Use only when you fully trust the commands being generated (e.g., well-tested automation scripts in disposable environments).
L130: 
L131: For destructive session slash commands (`/clear`, `/new` / `/reset`, `/undo`, `/quit --delete` — `/exit --delete` is an alias), the CLI also prompts for confirmation before running them. See cite38†Slash Commands — Confirmation prompts for destructive commands .
L132: ### Supervised-gateway lifecycle restrictioncite39†​ L133: 
L134: The terminal tool has a separate, non-overridable guard against stopping or restarting the gateway from inside its own supervised process. A self-restart can terminate the tool before it finishes and cause a supervisor/auto-resume loop. User approval, YOLO mode, and `force=True` do not bypass this guard.
L135: The guard also refuses process killers aimed at the interpreter image the gateway runs as — `taskkill /F /IM python.exe`, `taskkill /FI "IMAGENAME eq python.exe"`, `Stop-Process -Name python`, `pkill -9 python3`, `killall python`, `pkill -f python`, and name-derived kills such as `pgrep python | xargs kill` — because a supervised gateway is literally a `python` process and such a command takes it (and the agent's own turn) down.
L136: Kills scoped to a process the agent owns pass: the `proc_*` id of a background job (`process(action="kill", …)`) or an explicit PID (`taskkill /F /PID <pid>`, `kill <pid>`). Other image names (`taskkill /F /IM notepad.exe`) are unaffected. The guard is active under every generated launcher — systemd unit, launchd plist, s6 run script and the Windows Scheduled Task — via the `HERMES_SUPERVISED_CHILD` marker they export.
L137: On macOS, executed `launchctl submit` and `launchctl bootstrap` commands are restricted regardless of the job label. This is a conservative registration restriction intended to catch indirect restart helpers with neutral labels, not an inspection of the target plist. It also rejects independent scheduled jobs with `RunAtLoad=false` and no `KeepAlive` key; rejection does not establish that the job uses KeepAlive or controls Hermes.

L264: ### Approval Flow (Gateway/Messaging)cite46†​ L265:

L322: Safety rules:
L323:   * Nothing is ever applied automatically — the default run is read-only; only an explicit `--apply N[,M...]` writes to `config.yaml`.
L324:   * Destructive classes are never proposed, no matter how often they were approved: recursive deletes, `sudo`, disk/device writes, credential and system-config edits, pipe-to-shell, SQL DROP/TRUNCATE, process kills, and every hardline class are excluded outright. `rm -rf build/` approved 100 times still never yields an `rm` entry.
L325:   * Proposals already covered by your existing `command_allowlist` are skipped.
L326:   * Credentials inside mined commands are masked (`ghp_…`, `bot<id>:<token>` URLs, `KEY=value` assignments, bearer tokens) in both the printed `e.g.` examples and the `--json` payload, using the same redactor as terminal output. Masked text is never used as an allowlist pattern: a command whose glob would embed a credential (`TOKEN=… git …`) is proposed under its dangerous-class key instead. The session database itself still holds the command as it was executed.
L327: Useful flags: `--days N` (history window, default 90), `--min-count N` (minimum approvals to qualify, default 2), `--limit N`, and `--db PATH`.
L328: ## File Write Safetycite49†​ L329: 
L330: Before `write_file` or `patch` touches disk, Hermes checks the target path against a denylist and an optional sandbox. Blocked writes return an error to the agent immediately — there is no approval prompt and no way to override from the chat UI. The model may still claim the edit succeeded; when `display.file_mutation_verifier` is on (default), trust the cite50†file-mutation verifier footer over the assistant's closing summary.

For CI watchers the better pattern is still: the child returns the fact (PR number, SHA) and the parent launches its own watcher.
L319: ## Model Overridecite47†​ L320: 
L321: You can configure a different model for subagents via `config.yaml` — useful for delegating simple tasks to cheaper/faster models:
L322: 
L323:     `
L324: 
L325:     # In ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L326: 
L327:     delegation:
L328: 
L329:       model: "google/gemini-flash-2.0"    # Cheaper model for subagents
L330: 
L331:       provider: "openrouter"              # Optional: route subagents to a different provider
L332: 
L333:     `
L334: 
L335: If omitted, subagents use the same model as the parent.
L336: ### Cost strategy: frontier planner, inexpensive workerscite48†​ L337: Decomposing a problem into well-specified subtasks takes frontier-level judgment; executing a subtask that already comes with a clear goal, full context, and an output contract usually doesn't. Meanwhile the children are where the tokens go — a parallel batch of subagents typically burns the large majority of a run's total tokens, so the worker model is where the cost actually lives.
L338: Pinning `delegation.model` to an inexpensive model while your main session stays on a frontier model keeps the planning quality where it matters and cuts spend where the volume is:
L339: 
L340:     `
L341: 
L342:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L343: 
L344:     model:
L345: 
L346:       default: "your-frontier-model"     # parent (planner) stays on the frontier model
L347: 
L348:     delegation:
L349: 
L350:       model: "your-inexpensive-model"    # all delegate_task children run on this
L351: 
L352:       provider: "openrouter"             # optional: route children to a different provider
L353: 
L354:     `
L355: Resolution order: `delegation.base_url` (direct endpoint) takes precedence, then `delegation.provider` (full credential bundle resolved via the runtime provider system), and when neither is set children inherit the parent's provider and credentials; `delegation.model` applies in all cases, and when it is empty children inherit the parent's model.
L356: Setting `delegation.provider` alongside `delegation.base_url` keeps the explicit endpoint but carries that provider's request overrides and max output tokens into the child. An explicit `delegation.request_overrides` dict is honored on every branch and merges over those runtime-derived values (see cite49†Configuration below).
L357: Note that the pin is global: `delegate_task` has no per-task model parameter, so every child in a batch runs on the configured delegation model. For quality-sensitive subtasks that need a stronger model, either leave `delegation.model` unset for that session or hand the task to the cite50†kanban board , which does support a per-task model override.
L358: ## The `/review` Commandcite51†​ L359: 
L360: `/review` spawns an independent, full-privilege background subagent whose only job is to review the work your conversation just produced — a PR, a diff, code, documentation, a design. It works on every surface: CLI, TUI, the Desktop app, and every gateway messaging platform.
L361: 
L362:     `
L363: 
L364:     /review                       # review whatever the last 10 messages presented
L365: 
L366:     /review focus on security     # add extra instructions for the reviewer
L367: 
L368:     `
L369: What happens:
L370:   1. The last 10 user/assistant messages are snapshotted as the reviewer's starting evidence (tool output and system messages are excluded).
L371:   2. A reviewer subagent is dispatched on the same background delegation rail as `delegate_task` — it gets the full normal subagent toolset (terminal, web, files, browser...), so it actually opens the PR, reads the diff, and runs code rather than judging from the excerpt.
L372:   3. The reviewer inherits the primary agent's working context: any skills the primary agent had loaded (launch-preloaded or via `skill_view` during the session) are named in its briefing with an instruction to load them and judge the work against their conventions. Like every subagent, its system prompt also embeds the workspace's project context files (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules) as binding conventions.
L373:   4. When it finishes, its full review re-enters the same session as a normal background-subagent completion — your primary agent sees it and can act on it (fix the findings, push follow-ups, reply to you).
L374: The canonical flow: your main agent opens a PR, you type `/review`, and a second pair of eyes investigates it while you keep working; the review lands back in the chat addressed to the agent that created the PR.
L375: Dispatch prints only “Review started. Results will return here.” The live subagent viewer identifies the worker as Review: your focus (or Review recent work for bare `/review`), with a shortened single-line label; the reviewer still receives your full instructions. In the classic CLI, the dock above the composer shows elapsed time and latest activity; Ctrl+T (or F6) opens the roster with its model, transcript, steering, and stop controls.
L376: The same review label appears in the TUI and Desktop subagent viewers.
L377: ### Review modelcite52†​ L378: 
L379: By default the reviewer runs on your main model. To pin a dedicated review model, set `auxiliary.review` in `config.yaml`:
L380: 
L381:     `
L382: 
L383:     auxiliary:
L384: 
L385:       review:
L386: 
L387:         provider: openrouter               # or nous, anthropic, a direct base_url, ...
L388: 
L389:         model: anthropic/claude-opus-4.6   # a strong reviewer model
L390: 
L391:     `
L392: Credentials resolve exactly like a `delegation.provider` pin (full runtime-provider bundle: base_url, api key, api_mode). `provider: auto` with an empty `model` means "inherit the main agent's model" — the default.
L393: 
L394: `/review` is deliberately separate from `/refine`: `/refine` reviews the conversation to update memory and skills, `/review` reviews the work product the conversation created.
L395: ## Inherited Tool Accesscite53†​ L396: 
L397: `delegate_task` does not accept a model-facing `toolsets` parameter. Each subagent inherits the parent's enabled toolsets so the model cannot grant a child capabilities that the parent does not have. Configure the parent's tools before starting the conversation if delegated work needs additional capabilities.
L398: 
L399: Certain tools are blocked for subagents even when the parent has them:
L400:   * `delegate_task` — blocked for leaf subagents (the default). Retained for `role="orchestrator"` children, bounded by `max_spawn_depth` — see cite54†Depth Limit and Nested Orchestration below.
L401:   * `clarify` — subagents cannot interact with the user
L402:   * `memory` — no writes to shared persistent memory
L403:   * `send_message` — no cross-platform side effects
L404:   * `cronjob` — no scheduling more work in the parent's name
L405: Both roles retain `execute_code` (programmatic tool calling) so children can batch mechanical work.
L406: ## Max Iterationscite55†​ L407: 
L408: Each subagent has an iteration limit (default: 250) that controls how many tool-calling turns it can take. The limit is set globally in `config.yaml` and applies to every child; it is not a per-call parameter of `delegate_task`:
L409: 
L410:     `
L411: 
L412:     # In ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L413: 
L414:     delegation:
L415: 
L416:       max_iterations: 60   # lower it for fleets of simple tasks, raise it for long investigations
L417: 
L418:     `
L419: A child that exhausts its budget returns with `exit_reason: max_iterations` and `truncated: true`, so the parent can tell a budget stop from a completed task.
L420: ## Child Timeoutcite56†​ L421: 
L422: By default there is no wall-clock timeout on subagents. Children fail only from what they're actually doing — API errors, tool errors, or hitting their iteration budget — never from a delegation-level stopwatch. Earlier releases shipped a hard cap (300s, later 600s), which kept killing legitimately busy children mid-task: deep code reviews, large research fan-outs, and slow reasoning models routinely need more than 10 minutes while making steady progress the whole time.
L423: Genuinely stuck children are still detected on every runtime, with or without a configured cap: the heartbeat staleness monitor watches each child's progress signals (API calls, tool starts, activity-timestamp ticks).
L424: A child whose progress is completely frozen past the stale threshold — 450s idle between turns, 1200s while inside a tool — is interrupted and its wait is abandoned: the parent gets a `status: "timeout"` entry whose error reads `Subagent stopped making progress after N API call(s) — no activity for 450s (heartbeat stale threshold); the pending worker was abandoned.` The wait ends even in one-shot runs (`hermes chat -Q`, Bot Chat one-shot, cron) that have no gateway inactivity watchdog behind them, so a wedged child can no longer hold the turn or its session lease forever.
L425: An in-flight model wait still counts as progress — subagents refresh the activity clock while waiting on the provider, so a slow local / long-prefill completion is not treated as stalled.
L426: If you want a cap anyway (e.g. cost control on unattended cron-driven delegation), opt in per-install:
L427: 
L428:     `
L429: 
L430:     delegation:
L431: 
L432:       child_timeout_seconds: 0     # default: 0 = no timeout
L433: 
L434:       # child_timeout_seconds: 1800  # opt-in inactivity cap (floor 30s)
L435: 
L436:     `
L437: A positive value bounds inactivity, not total runtime: it is the longest a child may go with no progress (no completed API call, no tool change, no activity-clock tick) before it is abandoned. Every sign of progress restarts the window, so a child waiting on a multi-minute completion — the case that used to lose finished work — is never killed for taking long, while a child that has genuinely stopped moving is still caught (and an in-flight request is bounded independently by the per-call stale watchdog).

**Hermes documents useful primitives, but owner-bound action approval and safe restart recovery still need deployment proof.**

1. **Owner-only consequential approval.** In a test site, prepare Sahan’s purchase/message/deletion; have Nishank try the button, text approval, and a copied control. Then change the amount/recipient after Sahan approves. Expect wrong-owner rejection and fresh confirmation for changed details. **Documented:** Slack approval buttons cover dangerous commands and `execute_code`; security policy primarily evaluates shell commands. **Unknown:** complete browser-action approval and binding to resource owner, exact action, and audience. **Conditional gap:** add a narrow action gate only where the selected tools fail this test. [Slack approvals](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/slack/#using-commands-inside-threads-the-cmd-prefix), [approval policy](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/security/#dangerous-command-approval).

2. **Channel → owner DM → approved sharing.** Start a shared task requiring Sahan’s private account; complete private work in his DM; inspect channel messages and attachments. Approve one specific excerpt for one channel, then try changing destination/content or replaying permission. **Documented:** `send_message` supports Slack user IDs, DM conversations, channels, and attachments. **Unknown:** automatic owner-bound private handoff and a separate authorization gate for sharing. **Conditional gap:** controlled result routing if ordinary configuration cannot enforce this. [Slack delivery targets](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/slack/#sending-messages-and-media-send_message).

3. **Background responsiveness and cancellation ownership.** Run simultaneous private tasks and a shared task; verify prompt acknowledgement, progress, completion destinations, and owner cancellation. Try Nishank’s `!stop` against Sahan’s DM work. **Documented:** `/bg` runs independently and returns results to its originating chat. `/stop` intentionally can stop another authorized participant’s work within the same chat/thread. **Implication:** the private run must actually have private session ownership; a label inside shared history is insufficient. **Conditional gap:** fix run/control routing if the private run remains controllable from the channel. [Background sessions](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/#background-sessions), [stop scope](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/sessions/#shared-vs-isolated-group-sessions).

4. **Crash at the consequential-action boundary.** Restart immediately before submission, immediately after the website accepted it, and after completion but before Slack delivery. Inspect the website independently before resuming. Expect no duplicate submission and correct private delivery. **Documented:** completed delegation results persist for later delivery; running children do **not** resume after restart, and attempts become `unknown`. Delivery is at least once. **Conditional gap:** reconcile uncertain external state and track completed actions before retrying; durable chat history alone does not provide this. [Delegation durability](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/delegation/#durable-background-completions).

5. **Bounded execution and stale approvals.** Let an approval expire; restart with a pending card; cancel during browser work; test an intentionally slow task. Verify stale permission cannot execute and cancellation stops further actions. **Documented:** dangerous-command approval timeouts fail closed; delegation has iteration limits, but its configurable timeout bounds inactivity rather than total runtime. **Conditional gap:** enforce total runtime/spend limits and external-tool cancellation where configuration fails. [Approval timeout](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/security/#approval-timeout), [delegation limits](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/delegation/#child-timeout).

This is documentation review only; none of these tests has passed on a yyot deployment.
